title: After My Clinical Clerkship at the University of North Carolina Hospital
paragraphs: From April 2006, I did a two-month clinical clerkship at the University of North Carolina (UNC) Hospital in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on the East Coast of the United States. Nagoya University and the UNC School of Medicine have had exchanges, starting with an exchange student program, for more than ten years, and last year two seniors also studied there for two months. In the first month, I trained on the Coagulation consult team within Hematology/oncology. The team consisted of four people, the attending, the fellow, the resident and me, and since there were no changes in members for the month, we grew close to one another and I was taught very kindly and carefully. At first we started from a very elementary level, but from around the second or third week I was allowed to give presentations every day on new patients and patients under follow-up, and I was able to acquire basic history-taking and examination methods, ways of grasping patient information, and presentation methods. In the second month, I trained on the Infectious disease consultation team. Because the team was large, I had fewer chances to be directly involved with patients than in the first month, but the number of cases the team handled was more than double that of the first month, so when I read the charts of the patients the team was following from cover to cover every day and looked up in the literature the points I did not understand or was interested in, there was never enough time. Thanks to improved listening ability and taking in a large amount of medical information, I became able to follow the discussions on rounds far better than in the first month. As a point of reflection on the two months of clerkship, because my study of English listening in Japan had been insufficient, I could not do the interviews of new patients entirely by myself and always did them in pairs with the help of a resident or fellow. Compared with physical examination, chart writing and presentation, I think that interviewing patients is a field that requires far more everyday English conversation ability. I realised that in order to work as a doctor overseas, language ability is as important as professional ability as a doctor, or even more so. Here, I would like to give some of the things that left an impression during the clerkship, divided into matters concerning individual doctors and matters concerning the system.

First, regarding individual doctors, the following two points were impressive. The first is that history-taking, physical examination methods, chart writing and presentation methods are patterned and systematic. Because patterning makes everything take the same form no matter who does it, I had the impression that the contents of charts and presentations are easy to understand. The second is that they place great importance on EBM. Discussions about diagnosis and treatment of patients are always held on the basis of evidence. Also, when they fell into a situation in which evidence had not been established, they always searched PubMed for cases similar to the present patient, and if they found a usable paper, they adopted it. It was also impressive that among the doctors there are very many who have obtained a master of public health (MPH) degree and are highly interested in producing evidence. Next, I will give three points that impressed me about the system. The first is that the types of co-medical staff are extremely varied. Medical work is more finely divided than in Japan, and I had the impression that people in each profession work with a high level of expertise and professionalism. The second is that physician consultation services are well developed and it is taken for granted that one patient is seen by several departments. I had the impression that the threshold for consulting another department is lower than in Japan. The third is that in each department the number of years until one becomes fully qualified, such as so many years as resident and so many years as fellow, is clearly defined. Compared with Japan, I had the impression that it is easier for doctors to make plans for their own future careers. These two months at UNC were truly stimulating and fulfilling every day. I would like to take this opportunity to express my sincere thanks to the many people who supported this study abroad, beginning with Dean Dr. 浜口 and Dr. 小林孝彰 of the International Exchange Office.
